title: Beside the weeping
hookLine: sit with a grieving friend and sigh with them, but don't groan inside; some readers find this cool, others wise (Enchiridion 16)

cards: Lifeguards learn a hard rule early. When someone is drowning, you don't just leap in and grab them. A panicking swimmer can pull the rescuer under, and then there are two people in trouble instead of one.
You go in with a float, you stay on top of the water, and from there you can actually help. Grief can work like deep water.
A friend calls, sobbing, and it's easy to dive straight in, until you're crying too hard to hear what they need. Section sixteen of the handbook is about exactly this moment.

teach.b: When you see someone weeping in grief, Epictetus says, because a child has gone far away, or because they've lost their property, don't let the impression carry you off, as if they were truly in the grip of an outside evil.

teach.h: INSIDE: NOT THE EVENT, THE JUDGMENT.
teach.b: Have ready, he says, the thought: it isn't the event itself that crushes this person, since someone else meets the same event and isn't crushed. It's their judgment about it.
That's day three hundred thirty-seven, dogma, turned toward someone else.

And yet, he says, don't hesitate to sympathize with them in words, and even, if the moment calls for it, to sigh and groan along with them. Only take care not to groan inwardly as well. Sit with them.
Some people find this passage cool, even a little false: comforting someone while privately thinking their grief is a mistake.
Others find it wise and practical, the lifeguard's float: you stay steady enough to stay present, to bring soup on day fifteen, to call again in a month.
Epictetus himself doesn't tell you to say the inner sentence out loud. That would be cruel, and nothing in the text suggests it. Neighbors have their own words for the outward part.
Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James words: "weep with them that weep." Epictetus pairs that outward part with a steady one inside.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism comfort the grieving with real warmth in word and gesture while trying to stay inwardly steady, so they can keep showing up.

o: the Stoic who wrote down Epictetus' sayings
a Roman emperor who loved Epictetus' teaching
the writer of Romans: weep with them that weep

games.q: beside the weeping — tap the pairs.
p: stays on top of the water

s: Epictetus says to tell a grieving friend their grief is a mistake
the judgment is something you hold inside; he says sympathize in words.
he says you may even sigh and groan along with them
only take care not to groan inwardly as well.
all readers agree this passage is wise
some find it cool, others wise and practical.

games.q: your friend is weeping because their child has moved far away. what does section sixteen suggest?
o: tell them it's only their opinion.
sympathize aloud, and stay steady inside.
games.why: don't hesitate to sympathize, even to sigh with them, Epictetus says; just don't groan inwardly too.

practice: Bring to mind someone you know who is hurting right now, and picture sitting beside them, your face soft, real sympathy coming the way it would. Then, underneath, find your own feet: the floor, your breath going in and out, steady.
Warmth on the outside, ground on the inside, both at once.

wordCard.voice: Paul, who wrote weep with them that weep: sigh with a grieving friend, sympathize in words, but keep steady inside, so you can stay. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: with them, steady. Your warmth helps most when your feet stay on the floor. See you tomorrow.
